paper_title: DIY-MKG An LLM-Based Polyglot Language Learning System
caption: DIY-MKG reliably expands the vocabulary with low sensitivity to the language and the starting word. For each language, 10 opaque curves represent vocabulary sizes obtained from 10 different starting words, and one solid curve represents the average of the 10 curves. The standard deviations across languages and starting words are small, indicating fairness for all language learners. The diagonal gray line represents the upper-bound of vocabulary size, assuming all words in each iteration have not yet appeared in the vocabulary. While the real expansion rate is lower, the vocabulary does not saturate after 500 iterations. Therefore, DIY-MKG can reliably help the language learner to expand their vocabulary by consistently introducing new words.
model_annotation: This line plot illustrates the vocabulary size growth over the number of iterations for three languages—Spanish, Korean, and Japanese—using a DIY-MKG system. The x-axis, labeled “Number of Iterations,” ranges from 0 to 500 on a linear scale, with tick marks at intervals of 100. The y-axis, labeled “Vocabulary Size,” ranges from 0 to 5000 on a linear scale, with tick marks at intervals of 1000. For each language, a solid line represents the average vocabulary size across 10 different starting words, while 10 fainter, opaque curves behind each solid line represent the individual runs for those starting words. The Spanish vocabulary is shown by a solid blue line, the Korean vocabulary by a solid orange line, and the Japanese vocabulary by a solid green line. All three lines start at a vocabulary size of 0 at iteration 0 and increase steadily, ending at approximately 4000 for Spanish, 3500 for Korean, and 3200 for Japanese at iteration 500. Each line is accompanied by a shaded area around it indicating the spread of the 10 individual runs, which are visually very tight, suggesting low variance. A diagonal gray line runs from the origin to the top-right corner of the plot, representing the theoretical maximum vocabulary size if all new words were introduced at each iteration. The solid lines for all three languages lie below this diagonal, indicating that the actual expansion rate is slower than the theoretical upper bound, but they continue to grow without saturating even after 500 iterations.
